problem_plain: When many chips work together to train or run an AI model, they must constantly send each other partial results and stay in sync — each chip finishes its piece of the math, then everyone has to swap numbers before the next step can begin. The wires that carry this traffic have a fixed, physically limited capacity. As models and clusters grow, the volume of data that must move between chips grows faster than those wires can handle, so expensive chips sit idle, waiting for numbers to arrive rather than doing useful work.
why_plain: Physics sets hard limits: more wires cost more area and energy, and signals weaken over distance. You cannot simply add bandwidth the way you can add more math units. Meanwhile AI models keep growing, meaning more chips must share more data at once — the demand outpaces what physics cheaply allows.
approach_plain: Papers in this theme attack the bottleneck from three angles: reduce how much data needs to move at all (by sending only what matters, sending smaller numbers, or skipping unimportant values); move data more cleverly (by starting transfers early, matching the message pattern to the actual wiring, or letting chips share cached copies); and rebuild the wiring and switches themselves (new connection patterns, smarter switches that do useful work on data as it passes through, and dedicated fast links). The shared insight is that saving even one byte of traffic or one millisecond of idle time compounds across thousands of chips and billions of training steps.

groups.heading: Hiding communication time behind computation — sending and calculating at the same time
groups.explain: After a chip finishes its local arithmetic, it must send results to other chips before everyone can move on. If it simply waits, that waiting time is pure waste. The trick is to start sending early — breaking a large message into smaller pieces, sending the first piece while still computing the second, so the wiring and the math units are both kept busy at the same time. This requires a smart planner — a compiler or runtime — that knows exactly when each piece of data will be ready and schedules its delivery in advance.

papers.name: Concerto
papers.gloss: A code planner that automatically breaks large between-chip messages into pieces and overlaps sending them with ongoing math, so no chip just waits; works across any way of splitting a model across chips and matches or beats the best hand-tuned training frameworks.

papers.name: TileLink
papers.gloss: A programming tool that treats a small block of math and the data transfer it needs as one unit, then compiles both into a single run on the chip; achieves 1.17–20.76x speedup over approaches that do math and transfers one at a time, with roughly one-tenth the hand-written code.

papers.name: MeshSlice
papers.gloss: A method for splitting model math across chips arranged in a grid (like seats in a stadium) that breaks large group-sum messages into many tiny ones interleaved with the math itself, hiding most of the waiting time; 12–23% faster than prior methods on a cluster of 256 chips.

papers.name: Chimera
papers.gloss: Finds cases where splitting a model in multiple ways at once creates back-to-back between-chip messages that could be merged into one, then fuses them; delivers 1.32–1.58x faster forward passes on dedicated AI chips.

groups.heading: Smarter group messages — designing the sharing pattern to match the actual wires
groups.explain: A group message is when every chip in a cluster must both contribute to and receive a shared result — for example, adding up updates from all workers after each training batch. The simple approach treats the wiring as a black box and uses generic ring or tree patterns that often pile onto the same wires at once. A better approach designs the message pattern to follow the actual physical connections, so data flows with the grain of the wiring rather than against it, keeping every link fully used.

papers.name: TidalMesh
papers.gloss: A group-sum message pattern designed natively for chips arranged in a two-dimensional grid; it sends updates in wave patterns that follow the grid's rows and columns, achieving up to 24% better group-sum speed on a 64-chip 8-by-8 grid versus generic ring or tree patterns.

papers.name: Vocabulary Parallelism
papers.gloss: Spreads the lookup table that maps words to numbers evenly across all pipeline stages, cutting the number of between-chip sync points from three to one per pass; improves training throughput by 5–51% for large language models.

papers.name: vNPU
papers.gloss: Lets multiple AI workloads share one tightly wired AI chip by making the message routing and memory addressing aware of the physical wiring layout, so sharing does not scramble the connections; allows sharing up to 1.92x faster than naive splitting.

papers.name: PIMnet
papers.gloss: Builds a dedicated multi-level message network between units that do math inside the memory chips themselves, letting them sum results directly with each other instead of routing everything through the main processor; up to 85x faster on group-sum operations, 11.8x faster on real workloads.

groups.heading: Reducing how much data moves — sending less by being smarter about what matters
groups.explain: The simplest way to relieve a congested road is to put fewer vehicles on it. For chip networks this means sending only the data that is truly needed: skipping update values that are close to zero, reusing knowledge about which positions carry the biggest updates, removing duplicate requests, and rearranging which chip stores which data so fewer cross-chip trips are needed in the first place.

papers.name: Radius
papers.gloss: Notices that the positions of the largest weight updates stabilize after the first 15–20% of training and reuses those known positions to send only the values — not the positions — cutting between-chip traffic by up to 90% and speeding training 19% on a cluster of 128 chips.

papers.name: Frugal
papers.gloss: Makes training large recommendation models practical on cheap chips without fast direct chip-to-chip links by rearranging which rows of the lookup table live on which chip to minimize cross-chip trips, then compressing what does get sent and overlapping transfers with math.

papers.name: TRACI
papers.gloss: Adds small logic inside network switches that notices when many chips are asking for the same row of a lookup table at once and merges those requests into one trip, delivering the answer to all requesters together; targets recommendation models where access patterns are hard to predict.

papers.name: DiTile-DGNN
papers.gloss: A chip design for neural networks whose connections change over time; it figures out which data stays the same across time steps and avoids resending or recomputing it, cutting run time 23–56% and energy 71–84% versus prior chip designs.

papers.name: Mithril
papers.gloss: Assigns consecutive layers of a model to different chips so each chip processes the full graph for its own layers, rather than slicing the graph itself across chips; reduces per-round cross-chip traffic by up to the number of layers — as much as 22.9x less data moved and 7.16x faster training on ordinary network links.

groups.heading: Wiring patterns — physical connection layouts that scale without breaking the budget
groups.explain: How chips are physically connected determines how many hops a message must take and how often wires get congested. A simple two-dimensional grid of chips is cheap but requires many hops to cross; a fully connected design is fast but far too expensive at large scale. Researchers explore wiring patterns that add a few long-range shortcuts or reorganize how groups connect so data takes fewer hops at a fraction of the cost, then pair them with routing rules that exploit the new structure.

papers.name: Zettafly
papers.gloss: A two-level wiring layout for very large clusters: the lower level creates small groups where every chip can talk to every other at full speed, and the upper level links groups through a small number of shared long-range connections, keeping the maximum number of hops low while staying affordable.

papers.name: Ruche Networks
papers.gloss: Adds evenly spaced long-range bypass links to a standard two-dimensional grid so distant chips can reach each other in fewer hops; a detailed chip blueprint evaluation shows better energy and chip-area efficiency per unit of throughput versus standard grid and wraparound-grid wiring.

papers.name: EIGEN
papers.gloss: Builds a two-level wiring network on the silicon bridge that connects stacked chips together: one level uses a flexible switch for planned routes, the other uses a learning-based agent to reroute around congestion; cuts message delay between stacked chips up to 67% and the number of hops up to 54%.

papers.name: FRED
papers.gloss: Places small reconfigurable switches across a large wafer connecting hundreds of stacked AI chips; the switches can partly sum values as they pass through and route different kinds of traffic over separate non-overlapping paths; achieves 1.34–1.87x faster end-to-end training versus a plain two-dimensional grid wafer.

papers.name: NetCrafter
papers.gloss: Sits at the boundary between fast wiring inside a group of chips and slower wiring between groups; it packs partly filled messages together, drops messages fetched early that are no longer needed, and prioritizes time-critical messages; reduces effective waiting time at that boundary.

papers.name: NearFetch
papers.gloss: When one chip in a multi-chip module asks for data held by a distant chip, checks whether an intermediate chip already has a copy and delivers it from there instead; cuts the average amount of data crossing between modules by 43% and improves overall speed 52% on workloads where chips share data.

papers.name: Push Multicast
papers.gloss: When a shared memory bank serves one chip's request, it immediately pushes a copy to other chips it predicts will ask next, splitting the wiring cost across all future users at once; saves 33–43% of average wiring traffic in chips with 16 to 64 cores.

groups.heading: Making the network do useful work — not just move bytes
groups.explain: Traditional wiring just moves bytes from one place to another. Several papers propose making the wiring itself do useful work along the way: carrying out small read-and-update operations at the chip that already holds the data instead of shipping the data back and forth, handling memory requests at the lowest physical signal layer to cut delays, and removing the main processor from the path of handling incoming messages entirely.

papers.name: EDM
papers.gloss: Handles requests to read or write another chip's memory at the very lowest signaling layer of standard networking hardware, skipping all the normal packet-handling overhead above it; achieves roughly 300 nanoseconds of delay for a remote memory read — about ten times faster than the usual approach over standard networking.

papers.name: Delegato
papers.gloss: Instead of fetching data across the chip boundary just to update it and send it back, forwards the update instruction itself to the chip that already holds the data, which does the update in place; a single reuse signal from the local cache guides where to send it; 1.13x faster than the best previous approach.

papers.name: AccDirect
papers.gloss: Connects the network card directly to the chip's internal work-distribution hardware using the standard chip link, removing the main processor from the path of handing out incoming network tasks; cuts total processor energy by 10% while raising throughput 14–50%.

papers.name: Plaid
papers.gloss: A flexible chip design (a grid of programmable logic cells) where every three math units share one small local switch instead of each unit having its own full switching network; saves 43–46% of power and chip area versus standard designs while matching their speed.

groups.heading: Choosing how to split a model — division strategies that change what must be sent
groups.explain: How you divide a model across chips determines not just which chip does which math, but which chips must talk to which, how often, and how much data they exchange. Choosing a cleverer division — or inventing a new kind — can eliminate whole categories of between-chip messages without changing the model or the hardware at all.

papers.name: GraphPipe
papers.gloss: Treats a model's computation as a branching map of tasks rather than a single chain and runs independent branches on different chip groups at the same time; unlocks parallelism opportunities that strictly sequential splitting misses and improves overall throughput.

papers.name: Vela
papers.gloss: Trains a 50-billion-parameter model on ordinary cloud machines using standard networking hardware (rather than specialized expensive links), letting chips read each other's memory directly without involving the main processor; achieves roughly 80% of the ideal speed at 1,500-chip scale, proven over 2.5 years of real production use.

papers.name: C4
papers.gloss: Uses the regular timing of between-chip sync steps as a built-in health monitor — any deviation signals a broken chip immediately — and pre-plans traffic routes to avoid collisions; cuts the overhead caused by hardware failures by 30% and between-chip traffic cost by 15%.

papers.name: Titan
papers.gloss: An automated search tool for designing very large wafer-scale AI chips that jointly finds the best way to divide model computation and the best wiring configuration between chip tiles, pruning options that violate physical or reliability limits before wasting time on them.

groups.heading: Tools for measuring and simulating chip-to-chip wiring
groups.explain: Before you can build a better network, you need to measure the current one accurately and explore proposed alternatives without spending months building real hardware. These papers provide the measurement and simulation tools that make the rest of the research possible.

papers.name: LEGOSim
papers.gloss: A simulation framework that runs different chip simulators as separate parallel processes that only sync when they actually exchange a message — not every clock tick — cutting synchronization overhead up to 99.9% and simulating mixed-chip systems (combining different chip types) with under 4% error versus real hardware.

connect: Every paper in this theme answers the same physical fact: arithmetic inside one chip is cheap and fast, but sending a result to another chip is expensive and slow. Whether researchers are sending smaller numbers, redesigning how group messages travel, making wiring switches do partial sums on the fly, or rethinking which chip stores which data, they are all closing the gap between how fast chips can compute and how fast they can share what they computed — because until that gap closes, adding more chips delivers diminishing returns.
